items.stem: Which statement best explains why the number of seedlings in each group was an important constant when interpreting Figure 1?
choices: The 0.0-g/L group had the control number of seedlings, so seedling number was the dependent variable.
All groups began with the same number of seedlings, so differences in mean dry mass could be attributed more specifically to nitrogen rather than to different starting populations.
The number of seedlings increased as nitrogen concentration increased, allowing the two factors to be compared.
The 5.6-g mean dry mass in Figure 1 shows that every group began with 5.6 seedlings.
items.stimulus: Researchers grew bean seedlings for 14 days to test how nitrogen fertilizer affects growth. Each group began with seedlings of the same age and number, and the intended difference among groups was nitrogen concentration. Table 1 lists the treatment conditions, while Figure 1 shows the mean dry mass measured at the end of the experiment. The group receiving no nitrogen fertilizer provided a reference for evaluating the treated groups.
items.explanation: Table 1 indicates that every group began with the same number of seedlings. Holding starting population constant prevents unequal group size from providing an alternative explanation for differences in mean dry mass in Figure 1.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 indicates that every group began with the same number of seedlings. Holding starting population constant prevents unequal group size from providing an alternative explanation for differences in mean dry mass in Figure 1.
per_choice.trap: Choice A confuses a treatment condition with a measured variable; C incorrectly says the number varied with nitrogen; D confuses a dry-mass value with a count of seedlings.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: If the researchers had not included the 0 mg/L group, what important limitation would they have faced when interpreting Figure 1 and Figure 2?
choices: They could not determine how the responses compared with untreated Daphnia.
They could not calculate the temperature recorded for any caffeine group.
They could not compare heart rate with survival because the displays use different units.
They could not determine which caffeine concentration was highest.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested how caffeine concentration affected the heart rate and survival of Daphnia. Groups received 0, 2, 4, 8, or 16 mg/L caffeine; the 0 mg/L group served as the control. Temperature was held constant, and pH, water volume, and exposure time were also kept the same for all groups. Table 1 gives the recorded temperature for each concentration, Figure 1 shows mean heart rate after exposure, and Figure 2 shows the percentage surviving.
items.explanation: Without the 0 mg/L control, the researchers would lack untreated baseline values for heart rate and survival. They could still compare the caffeine groups with one another, but they could not determine whether caffeine changed either response relative to normal conditions.

per_choice.correct: Without the 0 mg/L control, the researchers would lack untreated baseline values for heart rate and survival. They could still compare the caffeine groups with one another, but they could not determine whether caffeine changed either response relative to normal conditions.
per_choice.trap: The control is not needed to calculate temperature or identify the highest concentration, and different units do not prevent separate comparisons of heart rate and survival.

items.stem: Which factor was held constant in Table 1, and why was keeping it constant important for this investigation?
choices: The number of germinated seeds was constant, providing a fixed measure of root length.
The temperature was 22°C for every treatment, helping isolate the effect of salt concentration.
The temperature increased from 0°C to 150°C, allowing the effect of salt to be measured.
The salt concentration was 22 mmol/L for every treatment, helping isolate the effect of temperature.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how sodium chloride concentration affects the early growth of radish seedlings. They placed 20 seeds in each dish and kept the dishes under the same light conditions; the 0 mmol/L dish was designated as the control. Table 1 lists the salt concentration, incubation temperature, and number of seeds that germinated. Figure 1 shows the mean root length measured after 7 days for each treatment.
items.explanation: The temperature column is 22°C in all four rows, while salt concentration changes. Keeping temperature constant reduces its possible influence on growth.

per_choice.correct: The temperature column is 22°C in all four rows, while salt concentration changes. Keeping temperature constant reduces its possible influence on growth.

items.stem: What is the primary purpose of the control group in this investigation, as supported by Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: To show that the highest salt concentration produces the greatest root length.
To provide a no-salt baseline for comparing germination and root length in the salt treatments.
To establish that all dishes were incubated at different temperatures.
To prove that every seed germinated when no salt was added.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how sodium chloride concentration affects the early growth of radish seedlings. They placed 20 seeds in each dish and kept the dishes under the same light conditions; the 0 mmol/L dish was designated as the control. Table 1 lists the salt concentration, incubation temperature, and number of seeds that germinated. Figure 1 shows the mean root length measured after 7 days for each treatment.
items.explanation: The 0 mmol/L group supplies the baseline: it can be compared with the salt-treated groups using both germination counts in Table 1 and root lengths in Figure 1.

per_choice.correct: The 0 mmol/L group supplies the baseline: it can be compared with the salt-treated groups using both germination counts in Table 1 and root lengths in Figure 1.
per_choice.trap: The first choice reverses the downward trend in Figure 1, the third misreads the constant temperature column, and the fourth misreads the control's germination count of 18 out of 20.

items.stem: A student claims that the difference in root length between the 50 and 100 mmol/L groups was caused by different incubation temperatures. Which evidence from Table 1 and Figure 1 best contradicts the claim?
choices: The 100 mmol/L group had a shorter root length than the 0 mmol/L group.
Both groups were incubated at 22°C, but their mean root lengths were 35 mm and 24 mm, respectively.
The 50 mmol/L group had 15 germinated seeds, whereas the 150 mmol/L group had 4.
The 0 mmol/L group was incubated at 22°C and had a mean root length of 42 mm.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how sodium chloride concentration affects the early growth of radish seedlings. They placed 20 seeds in each dish and kept the dishes under the same light conditions; the 0 mmol/L dish was designated as the control. Table 1 lists the salt concentration, incubation temperature, and number of seeds that germinated. Figure 1 shows the mean root length measured after 7 days for each treatment.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows that both the 50 and 100 mmol/L groups had the same temperature, 22°C. Figure 1 shows that their root lengths nevertheless differed, so their salt concentrations—not different temperatures—could explain the comparison.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 shows that both the 50 and 100 mmol/L groups had the same temperature, 22°C. Figure 1 shows that their root lengths nevertheless differed, so their salt concentrations—not different temperatures—could explain the comparison.
per_choice.trap: The other choices use a different pair of treatments, compare germination rather than the claimed root lengths, or show a general trend without ruling out temperature as the cause of the specific difference.

items.stem: According to the passage, what factor did the researchers change among the groups?
choices: The number of light hours
The type of soil
The amount of nitrogen fertilizer
The volume of water
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how nitrogen fertilizer affects the growth of lettuce seedlings. They placed equal numbers of seedlings in four groups and gave each group a different amount of fertilizer. All groups received the same soil, 12 hours of light per day, and the same volume of water. The group receiving no fertilizer served as the control group, allowing the researchers to compare fertilizer-treated plants with plants grown without fertilizer.
items.explanation: The passage states that each group received a different amount of fertilizer.

per_choice.correct: The passage states that each group received a different amount of fertilizer.
per_choice.trap: The other choices are factors that were kept the same.

items.stem: A student claims that the blue group had the largest bar in Figure 1 simply because it contained more algae at the beginning. Which evidence from both displays most directly evaluates this claim?
choices: Table 1 gives the blue group an initial density of 2.0, and Figure 1 gives it the largest net increase of 4.8.
Table 1 gives the red group a temperature of 25, and Figure 1 gives it a net increase of 2.4, showing that temperature caused its lower growth.
Table 1 gives the blue group an irradiance of 100, and Figure 1 gives it a net increase of 4.8, showing that irradiance was higher for blue.
Table 1 gives the white group an initial density of 2.0, and Figure 1 gives it a net increase of 3.0, showing that white began with fewer cells.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether light wavelength affects the seven-day growth of Chlorella algae. Equal volumes of cultures were placed under white, blue, green, or red LEDs; irradiance, temperature, and initial cell density were kept the same across groups. The white-light culture served as the control because it provided a broad-spectrum reference for comparison with the colored-light treatments. Table 1 gives the culture conditions and final densities, while Figure 1 shows the net increase in cell density calculated from those measurements.
items.explanation: The blue and white groups both began at 2.0 × 10^6 cells/mL, so the blue group's larger 4.8 increase cannot be attributed to a larger starting population.

per_choice.correct: The blue and white groups both began at 2.0 × 10^6 cells/mL, so the blue group's larger 4.8 increase cannot be attributed to a larger starting population.
per_choice.trap: The other choices read a value from the correct display but incorrectly treat a shared constant, or a different group's value, as evidence of a starting difference or causal effect.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Why is the white-light group more useful as a control than the red-light group for interpreting the colored-light results in Figure 1?
choices: The blue group supplies the control because its 4.8 increase is the largest value, making it the most sensitive reference.
The red group supplies the control because its 2.4 increase is the smallest value, making it the best low-growth baseline.
The white group supplies the stated broad-spectrum reference, so its 3.0 increase can be compared with colored groups tested at the same irradiance and initial density.
All three colored groups together supply the control because their irradiance values in Table 1 are identical.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether light wavelength affects the seven-day growth of Chlorella algae. Equal volumes of cultures were placed under white, blue, green, or red LEDs; irradiance, temperature, and initial cell density were kept the same across groups. The white-light culture served as the control because it provided a broad-spectrum reference for comparison with the colored-light treatments. Table 1 gives the culture conditions and final densities, while Figure 1 shows the net increase in cell density calculated from those measurements.
items.explanation: The passage identifies white light as the broad-spectrum reference, and Table 1 shows that its irradiance and initial density match those of the colored groups; Figure 1 then provides the growth comparison.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Which pair of columns in Table 1 is most important for determining whether the greater blue-light increase in Figure 1 can be attributed to light color rather than either unequal light dose or unequal starting population?
choices: Temperature and volume
Final density and net increase
Light and final density
Irradiance and initial density
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether light wavelength affects the seven-day growth of Chlorella algae. Equal volumes of cultures were placed under white, blue, green, or red LEDs; irradiance, temperature, and initial cell density were kept the same across groups. The white-light culture served as the control because it provided a broad-spectrum reference for comparison with the colored-light treatments. Table 1 gives the culture conditions and final densities, while Figure 1 shows the net increase in cell density calculated from those measurements.
items.explanation: Irradiance measures the amount of light delivered, and initial density measures the starting population; both are 100 and 2.0, respectively, for every group. Figure 1 can therefore be compared without those two confounders.

per_choice.trap: The alternatives use other columns that are constant, or they include the treatment variable or an outcome rather than both possible confounding factors named in the question.

items.stem: Which statement best combines the control comparison with the standardized conditions to support the conclusion that blue wavelength enhanced growth relative to the baseline?
choices: Blue produced a 4.8 increase versus the white control's 3.0, while Table 1 shows both groups had irradiance of 100 and initial density of 2.0.
White produced a 3.0 increase versus green's 3.6, while Table 1 shows that white began with fewer cells than green.
Red produced a 2.4 increase versus blue's 4.8, while Table 1 shows that red and blue had different temperatures.
Blue produced a 4.8 increase versus red's 2.4, while Table 1 shows that blue had a higher irradiance than red.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether light wavelength affects the seven-day growth of Chlorella algae. Equal volumes of cultures were placed under white, blue, green, or red LEDs; irradiance, temperature, and initial cell density were kept the same across groups. The white-light culture served as the control because it provided a broad-spectrum reference for comparison with the colored-light treatments. Table 1 gives the culture conditions and final densities, while Figure 1 shows the net increase in cell density calculated from those measurements.
items.explanation: The blue group exceeded the designated white control by 1.8 × 10^6 cells/mL, and the table confirms that irradiance and starting density were matched between them.

per_choice.correct: The blue group exceeded the designated white control by 1.8 × 10^6 cells/mL, and the table confirms that irradiance and starting density were matched between them.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Which statement best explains why the water volume in Table 1 was an important constant when interpreting Figure 1?
choices: The 0.0-g/L group received 25 mL/day, so water volume was the control group's dependent variable.
All groups received 25 mL/day, so differences in dry mass could be attributed more specifically to nitrogen rather than to different water supplies.
Water volume increased as nitrogen concentration increased, allowing the two factors to be compared.
The 5.6-g mean dry mass in Figure 1 shows that water volume was held constant at 5.6 mL/day.
items.stimulus: Researchers grew bean seedlings for 14 days to test how nitrogen fertilizer affects growth. Each group began with seedlings of the same age and number, and the intended difference among groups was nitrogen concentration. Table 1 lists the treatment conditions, while Figure 1 shows the mean dry mass measured at the end of the experiment. The group receiving no nitrogen fertilizer provided a reference for evaluating the treated groups.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows 25 mL/day for every nitrogen treatment. Holding water constant prevents unequal watering from providing an alternative explanation for the dry-mass differences in Figure 1.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 shows 25 mL/day for every nitrogen treatment. Holding water constant prevents unequal watering from providing an alternative explanation for the dry-mass differences in Figure 1.
per_choice.trap: Choice A confuses a treatment condition with a measured variable; C reads the y-axis value as a water volume; D reverses the constant water values in Table 1.

items.stem: To estimate the change in mean dry mass associated specifically with adding 1.0 g/L nitrogen relative to no nitrogen, which two Figure 1 bars should be compared, and why?
choices: The 0.0-g/L bar and the 1.0-g/L bar, because Table 1 identifies these as the reference and the specified nitrogen treatment while keeping the other listed conditions equal.
The 0.5-g/L bar and the 2.0-g/L bar, because they are the two treatments with the greatest separation in nitrogen concentration.
The 0.0-g/L bar and the 2.0-g/L bar, because the highest treatment gives the clearest estimate of the effect of any nitrogen.
The 25-mL/day and 12-h/day entries in Table 1, because those are the two constant conditions associated with the 1.0-g/L group.

The group receiving no nitrogen fertilizer provided a reference for evaluating the treated groups.
items.explanation: The requested comparison is no nitrogen versus 1.0 g/L nitrogen: Figure 1 gives 3.2 g and 5.6 g, respectively. Table 1 confirms that water, light, and temperature are the same for those rows.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: A researcher predicts that mean dry mass will increase whenever nitrogen concentration increases. Which observation most directly contradicts that prediction without introducing a difference in the listed control conditions?
choices: Mean dry mass falls from 5.6 g at 1.0 g/L to 4.9 g at 2.0 g/L, even though Table 1 shows the same water, light, and temperature.
Mean dry mass rises from 3.2 g at 0.0 g/L to 4.8 g at 0.5 g/L.
Mean dry mass falls from 25 g at 1.0 g/L to 12 g at 2.0 g/L because the water and light values decrease.
Mean dry mass rises from 4.8 g at 0.5 g/L to 5.6 g at 1.0 g/L.
items.stimulus: Researchers grew bean seedlings for 14 days to test how nitrogen fertilizer affects growth. Each group began with seedlings of the same age and number, and the intended difference among groups was nitrogen concentration. Table 1 lists the treatment conditions, while Figure 1 shows the mean dry mass measured at the end of the experiment. The group receiving no nitrogen fertilizer provided a reference for evaluating the treated groups.
items.explanation: Figure 1 shows a decrease from 5.6 g at 1.0 g/L to 4.9 g at 2.0 g/L. Table 1 shows that the other listed conditions remain constant, so this is the observation that contradicts a continuously increasing relationship.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 shows a decrease from 5.6 g at 1.0 g/L to 4.9 g at 2.0 g/L. Table 1 shows that the other listed conditions remain constant, so this is the observation that contradicts a continuously increasing relationship.
per_choice.trap: Choices B and D describe increases rather than contradictions; D treats Table 1's water and light entries as dry-mass values and reverses their constant pattern.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Suppose a follow-up group receives 2.0 g/L nitrogen and 35 mL/day of water instead of the 25 mL/day shown for that treatment in Table 1. If its dry mass differs from the 2.0-g/L bar in Figure 1, what conclusion is justified?
choices: The difference cannot be attributed to nitrogen alone because both nitrogen and water conditions differ between the follow-up group and the original 2.0-g/L group.
The difference cannot be caused by water because the original no-nitrogen group is a control group.
The difference must be caused by nitrogen because the follow-up group still uses the highest nitrogen concentration.
The difference can be attributed to nitrogen alone because Figure 1 shows that dry mass is highest at 1.0 g/L.
items.stimulus: Researchers grew bean seedlings for 14 days to test how nitrogen fertilizer affects growth. Each group began with seedlings of the same age and number, and the intended difference among groups was nitrogen concentration. Table 1 lists the treatment conditions, while Figure 1 shows the mean dry mass measured at the end of the experiment. The group receiving no nitrogen fertilizer provided a reference for evaluating the treated groups.
items.explanation: The original 2.0-g/L group had 25 mL/day, whereas the follow-up group has 35 mL/day. A comparison between them changes two factors, so the effect of nitrogen cannot be isolated.

per_choice.correct: The original 2.0-g/L group had 25 mL/day, whereas the follow-up group has 35 mL/day. A comparison between them changes two factors, so the effect of nitrogen cannot be isolated.
per_choice.trap: Choice C focuses on the nitrogen row but ignores the changed water condition; C assumes a control group eliminates confounding in a new comparison; D uses the peak in Figure 1 as if it controlled the follow-up treatment.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Which factor was held constant for all groups, according to Table 1?
choices: The mean number of leaves
The daily light exposure
The final seedling height
The compost tea concentration
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether compost tea affects the growth of bean seedlings. Groups received compost tea at different concentrations, while the volume of solution, light exposure, temperature, and starting height were kept the same. Table 1 lists the treatment conditions, Figure 1 shows mean seedling height over time, and Figure 2 shows the mean number of leaves at the end of the study. The 0 mL/L group received water without compost tea.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows that every group received 12 hours of light per day, whereas compost tea concentration was changed and the other two quantities were measured outcomes.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Why was the 0 mL/L group included, based on Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: To provide a baseline height for comparing seedlings that received compost tea
To provide a second group that received the same compost tea concentration
To keep the amount of solution different from that of the other groups
To show that the greatest compost tea concentration produced the shortest seedlings
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether compost tea affects the growth of bean seedlings. Groups received compost tea at different concentrations, while the volume of solution, light exposure, temperature, and starting height were kept the same. Table 1 lists the treatment conditions, Figure 1 shows mean seedling height over time, and Figure 2 shows the mean number of leaves at the end of the study. The 0 mL/L group received water without compost tea.
items.explanation: Table 1 identifies 0 mL/L as the group receiving no compost tea, and Figure 1 provides its growth pattern as the baseline for comparison with the treated groups.

items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether compost tea affects the growth of bean seedlings. Groups received compost tea at different concentrations, while the volume of solution, light exposure, temperature, and starting height were kept the same. Table 1 lists the treatment conditions, Figure 1 shows mean seedling height over time, and Figure 2 shows the mean number of leaves at the end of the study. The 0 mL/L group received water without compost tea.
items.explanation: At day 12, the 50 mL/L seedlings averaged 18.4 cm and the 0 mL/L seedlings averaged 14.0 cm. The difference is 18.4 - 14.0 = 4.4 cm.

per_choice.correct: At day 12, the 50 mL/L seedlings averaged 18.4 cm and the 0 mL/L seedlings averaged 14.0 cm. The difference is 18.4 - 14.0 = 4.4 cm.
per_choice.trap: The 3.6 cm choice comes from subtracting the 75 mL/L value from the 50 mL/L value; 9.0 is the leaf count for the 50 mL/L group in Figure 2.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: A new trial gives all groups 8 hours of light per day instead of the amount listed in Table 1. Which conclusion is most appropriate when comparing its results with Figure 1?
choices: Any difference must be caused only by compost tea concentration
The new trial tests compost tea concentration under a different light condition
The new trial can be compared directly because light exposure was not measured
The new trial is a control because its seedlings receive less light
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether compost tea affects the growth of bean seedlings. Groups received compost tea at different concentrations, while the volume of solution, light exposure, temperature, and starting height were kept the same. Table 1 lists the treatment conditions, Figure 1 shows mean seedling height over time, and Figure 2 shows the mean number of leaves at the end of the study. The 0 mL/L group received water without compost tea.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows that 12 hours of light was held constant in the original study. Changing it to 8 hours introduces a second experimental difference, so the new trial tests compost tea under a different light condition.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 shows that 12 hours of light was held constant in the original study. Changing it to 8 hours introduces a second experimental difference, so the new trial tests compost tea under a different light condition.
per_choice.trap: A student may call the 8-hour group a control because it differs from the original, but a control is a comparison condition, not simply any changed condition.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Which factor was held constant among the trials in Table 1 and also held constant among the series being compared in Figure 1, making the caffeine concentrations the intended difference between those series?
choices: The temperature range used in Figure 2
The caffeine concentration
The carbon dioxide volume at 30 minutes
The fermentation temperature
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether caffeine concentration affects carbon dioxide production by yeast fermenting sugar. Four trials used different caffeine concentrations, while the sugar concentration, yeast volume, and temperature were controlled as shown in Table 1. Figure 1 shows carbon dioxide production over 30 minutes for the Table 1 trials, and Figure 2 shows 30-minute carbon dioxide production at several temperatures and caffeine concentrations. The trial containing no caffeine served as the control.
items.explanation: Table 1 lists 25 C for every trial, and Figure 1 compares the Table 1 trials at that same temperature. Caffeine is the changing factor, whereas the 30-minute CO2 values are outcomes and the temperature range belongs to Figure 2.

per_choice.trap: Choosing caffeine confuses the manipulated variable with a constant; choosing the 30-minute value or Figure 2's range uses an outcome or a feature of the wrong display.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Why is Trial 1 a more appropriate control for the 2.0 mg/mL treatment in Figure 1 than Trial 2 is?
choices: Trial 2 uses a lower caffeine concentration, so it controls for the temperature variation in Figure 2
Trial 1 has no caffeine but matches Trial 4 in temperature, sugar, and yeast volume
Trial 1 has the highest CO2 production and therefore represents the strongest treatment
Trial 2 has no caffeine at 30 minutes, whereas Trial 1 has 44 mL of CO2
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether caffeine concentration affects carbon dioxide production by yeast fermenting sugar. Four trials used different caffeine concentrations, while the sugar concentration, yeast volume, and temperature were controlled as shown in Table 1. Figure 1 shows carbon dioxide production over 30 minutes for the Table 1 trials, and Figure 2 shows 30-minute carbon dioxide production at several temperatures and caffeine concentrations. The trial containing no caffeine served as the control.
items.explanation: Trial 1 is the zero-caffeine baseline, and Table 1 shows that it has the same 25 C temperature, sugar concentration, and yeast volume as Trial 4. Thus a difference in Figure 1 can be compared with the absence of caffeine rather than with another caffeine treatment.

per_choice.correct: Trial 1 is the zero-caffeine baseline, and Table 1 shows that it has the same 25 C temperature, sugar concentration, and yeast volume as Trial 4. Thus a difference in Figure 1 can be compared with the absence of caffeine rather than with another caffeine treatment.
per_choice.trap: The other choices use a measured result as the definition of a control, misidentify Trial 2 as caffeine-free, or bring in the temperature variation from Figure 2 even though Figure 1 uses 25 C.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by combining Figure 1 with Figure 2, assuming the sugar and yeast conditions in Table 1 were maintained for all measurements?
choices: Caffeine lowers CO2 production at 25 C, but its effect cannot be separated from temperature because Figure 1 uses several temperatures
The control is effective only at 25 C because the zero-caffeine line is shown in Figure 1 but not in Figure 2
Caffeine lowers CO2 production at each tested temperature, while 25 C produces more CO2 than 15 C but less than 35 C at every listed caffeine concentration
Temperature has no effect because the 2.0 mg/mL treatment produces less CO2 than the control in both figures
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether caffeine concentration affects carbon dioxide production by yeast fermenting sugar. Four trials used different caffeine concentrations, while the sugar concentration, yeast volume, and temperature were controlled as shown in Table 1. Figure 1 shows carbon dioxide production over 30 minutes for the Table 1 trials, and Figure 2 shows 30-minute carbon dioxide production at several temperatures and caffeine concentrations. The trial containing no caffeine served as the control.
items.explanation: Figure 1 shows that, at the controlled 25 C temperature, increasing caffeine is associated with less CO2. Figure 2 shows the same downward caffeine pattern at 15, 25, and 35 C, and at each caffeine concentration the 25 C series lies between the 15 C and 35 C series.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 shows that, at the controlled 25 C temperature, increasing caffeine is associated with less CO2. Figure 2 shows the same downward caffeine pattern at 15, 25, and 35 C, and at each caffeine concentration the 25 C series lies between the 15 C and 35 C series.
per_choice.trap: The first choice falsely says Figure 1 uses several temperatures; the third reverses the evidence about temperature; the fourth ignores the zero-caffeine points in Figure 2.

items.stem: Suppose the researchers discovered that the yeast volume in Trial 4 was accidentally 6 mL instead of the 5 mL listed in Table 1. Which comparison would then be least valid as evidence that caffeine alone caused the difference in Figure 1?
choices: The comparison of the 15 C and 35 C series in Figure 2
The comparison of Trial 2 with Trial 3
The comparison of Trial 1 with Trial 2
The comparison of Trial 1 with Trial 4
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether caffeine concentration affects carbon dioxide production by yeast fermenting sugar. Four trials used different caffeine concentrations, while the sugar concentration, yeast volume, and temperature were controlled as shown in Table 1. Figure 1 shows carbon dioxide production over 30 minutes for the Table 1 trials, and Figure 2 shows 30-minute carbon dioxide production at several temperatures and caffeine concentrations. The trial containing no caffeine served as the control.
items.explanation: Trial 1 and Trial 4 are intended to differ only in caffeine concentration, but the newly discovered yeast-volume difference adds a second changing factor. The Trial 1–Trial 4 comparison would therefore not isolate caffeine. The other listed comparisons do not involve the altered Trial 4 volume.

per_choice.trap: Choosing Trial 2 versus Trial 3 overlooks that both still use 5 mL of yeast; choosing the Figure 2 comparison confuses a temperature comparison with the contaminated Table 1 trial.

items.stem: Which condition served as the control group, and why was it useful? Use Table 1 and Figure 1.
choices: 0 mg/L, because it provided growth and oxygen values without added copper sulfate
0.5 mg/L, because it was the lowest concentration that contained copper sulfate
1 mg/L, because it was the middle concentration tested
2 mg/L, because it produced the strongest treatment effect
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how copper sulfate concentration affects duckweed growth in two experiments. In Experiment 1, each container began with 10 fronds in 100 mL of nutrient solution and was kept at 22°C under 12 hours of light per day; only the copper sulfate concentration varied. Experiment 2 used the same concentrations and starting conditions but measured oxygen production after 24 hours. Table 1 shows frond counts from Experiment 1, Figure 1 shows oxygen production from Experiment 2, and Figure 2 shows the percentage of fronds surviving after 5 days.
items.explanation: The 0 mg/L condition had no added copper sulfate and supplied the baseline final-frond count and oxygen production for comparison with treated groups.

per_choice.correct: The 0 mg/L condition had no added copper sulfate and supplied the baseline final-frond count and oxygen production for comparison with treated groups.
per_choice.trap: The 0.5 mg/L choice confuses the lowest treatment concentration with the no-treatment control; the 2 mg/L choice identifies the strongest treatment rather than the baseline.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Compared with the control, approximately what percentage decrease in oxygen production occurred at 1 mg/L copper sulfate? Use Figure 1.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how copper sulfate concentration affects duckweed growth in two experiments. In Experiment 1, each container began with 10 fronds in 100 mL of nutrient solution and was kept at 22°C under 12 hours of light per day; only the copper sulfate concentration varied. Experiment 2 used the same concentrations and starting conditions but measured oxygen production after 24 hours. Table 1 shows frond counts from Experiment 1, Figure 1 shows oxygen production from Experiment 2, and Figure 2 shows the percentage of fronds surviving after 5 days.
items.explanation: Oxygen production decreased from 12 mL in the control to 7 mL at 1 mg/L. The decrease is 5/12, or approximately 42%.

per_choice.correct: Oxygen production decreased from 12 mL in the control to 7 mL at 1 mg/L. The decrease is 5/12, or approximately 42%.
per_choice.trap: The 25% choice treats the 5 mL decrease as a fraction of 20, and 50% rounds the decrease too far; 75% reverses the comparison with the remaining amount.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Of the variables recorded in Table 1, which factor was held constant so that differences across the caffeine concentrations could be attributed to caffeine rather than to that factor?
choices: Percentage surviving
Heart rate
Caffeine concentration
Temperature
items.stimulus: Researchers tested how caffeine concentration affected the heart rate and survival of Daphnia. Groups received 0, 2, 4, 8, or 16 mg/L caffeine; the 0 mg/L group served as the control. Temperature was held constant, and pH, water volume, and exposure time were also kept the same for all groups. Table 1 gives the recorded temperature for each concentration, Figure 1 shows mean heart rate after exposure, and Figure 2 shows the percentage surviving.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows 21°C for every caffeine concentration, whereas caffeine concentration is the factor that changes.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 shows 21°C for every caffeine concentration, whereas caffeine concentration is the factor that changes.
per_choice.trap: Choosing caffeine concentration confuses the manipulated variable with a controlled variable; heart rate and survival are measured responses.

items.stem: Why was the 0 mg/L group necessary when interpreting both Figure 1 and Figure 2?
choices: It provided a baseline for judging whether exposure to caffeine changed heart rate or survival.
It showed the maximum possible heart rate and survival for every Daphnia group.
It allowed the researchers to compare heart rate and survival using the same units.
It confirmed that temperature increased as caffeine concentration increased.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested how caffeine concentration affected the heart rate and survival of Daphnia. Groups received 0, 2, 4, 8, or 16 mg/L caffeine; the 0 mg/L group served as the control. Temperature was held constant, and pH, water volume, and exposure time were also kept the same for all groups. Table 1 gives the recorded temperature for each concentration, Figure 1 shows mean heart rate after exposure, and Figure 2 shows the percentage surviving.
items.explanation: The 0 mg/L values, 182 bpm in Figure 1 and 100% in Figure 2, provide untreated baselines against which the caffeine groups can be compared.

per_choice.correct: The 0 mg/L values, 182 bpm in Figure 1 and 100% in Figure 2, provide untreated baselines against which the caffeine groups can be compared.
per_choice.trap: The control does not establish a maximum for all groups, and neither display shows temperature changing or converts the responses to the same units.

items.stem: A follow-up group is exposed to 10 mg/L caffeine at 25°C. To determine whether its result can be compared with the original concentration trend as a test of caffeine's effect, which arrangement is required for the follow-up control and treatment groups?
choices: The control at 21°C and 0 mg/L, with the treatment at 25°C and 10 mg/L
Both groups at 25°C, with the control at 0 mg/L and the treatment at 10 mg/L
Both groups at 25°C, with the control at 10 mg/L and the treatment at 0 mg/L
Both groups at 21°C, with the control at 0 mg/L and the treatment at 10 mg/L
items.stimulus: Researchers tested how caffeine concentration affected the heart rate and survival of Daphnia. Groups received 0, 2, 4, 8, or 16 mg/L caffeine; the 0 mg/L group served as the control. Temperature was held constant, and pH, water volume, and exposure time were also kept the same for all groups. Table 1 gives the recorded temperature for each concentration, Figure 1 shows mean heart rate after exposure, and Figure 2 shows the percentage surviving.
items.explanation: The new treatment is at 25°C, so its 0 mg/L control must also be at 25°C; otherwise caffeine concentration and temperature would change together. The original Table 1 establishes that each concentration comparison uses the same temperature within that comparison.

per_choice.correct: The new treatment is at 25°C, so its 0 mg/L control must also be at 25°C; otherwise caffeine concentration and temperature would change together. The original Table 1 establishes that each concentration comparison uses the same temperature within that comparison.
per_choice.trap: Choice D compares the new treatment with the original temperature rather than matching the follow-up control; choice A confounds temperature with caffeine, and choice C reverses control and treatment.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: At 8 mg/L caffeine, which response shows the greater percentage decrease from its own 0 mg/L control value? Use both Figure 1 and Figure 2, and calculate each decrease relative to its corresponding control.
choices: Heart rate, by 0.0%
Survival, by 15.4%
Survival, by 12.0%
Heart rate, by 15.4%
items.stimulus: Researchers tested how caffeine concentration affected the heart rate and survival of Daphnia. Groups received 0, 2, 4, 8, or 16 mg/L caffeine; the 0 mg/L group served as the control. Temperature was held constant, and pH, water volume, and exposure time were also kept the same for all groups. Table 1 gives the recorded temperature for each concentration, Figure 1 shows mean heart rate after exposure, and Figure 2 shows the percentage surviving.
items.explanation: Heart rate decreases from 182 to 154 bpm, a decrease of 28/182 × 100 ≈ 15.4%. Survival decreases from 100% to 88%, or 12.0%. Thus heart rate has the greater proportional decrease.

per_choice.correct: Heart rate decreases from 182 to 154 bpm, a decrease of 28/182 × 100 ≈ 15.4%. Survival decreases from 100% to 88%, or 12.0%. Thus heart rate has the greater proportional decrease.
per_choice.trap: The 12.0% value is the survival decrease, while 15.4% requires dividing the heart-rate change by 182 rather than treating 28 bpm as a percentage.

items.stem: According to Table 1, which factor was held constant in all 4 trials?
choices: CO2 collected
Sugar concentration
Trial number
Temperature of 25°C
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how sugar concentration affects the amount of carbon dioxide produced by yeast. Each mixture contained the same amount of yeast and liquid and was kept at 25°C for 20 minutes. A mixture containing no sugar served as the control group. Table 1 lists the trial conditions and measurements, Figure 1 graphs the measurements, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used to collect the gas.
items.explanation: The temperature column shows 25°C for every trial.

items.stem: Why was the 0% sugar mixture in Table 1 included as a control group?
choices: To show the longest collection time
To increase the temperature of the mixtures
To measure the amount of yeast used
To provide a baseline for CO2 production without added sugar
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how sugar concentration affects the amount of carbon dioxide produced by yeast. Each mixture contained the same amount of yeast and liquid and was kept at 25°C for 20 minutes. A mixture containing no sugar served as the control group. Table 1 lists the trial conditions and measurements, Figure 1 graphs the measurements, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used to collect the gas.

choices: CO2 collected (mL)
Temperature (C)
Trial number

items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how sugar concentration affects the amount of carbon dioxide produced by yeast. Each mixture contained the same amount of yeast and liquid and was kept at 25°C for 20 minutes. A mixture containing no sugar served as the control group. Table 1 lists the trial conditions and measurements, Figure 1 graphs the measurements, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used to collect the gas.
items.explanation: Figure 2 labels the collector for CO2 in milliliters, matching the CO2 collected (mL) column in Table 1.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Suppose the researchers moved only the 4 mg/L flask farther from the lamp while leaving its labeled copper sulfate concentration unchanged. Why would this change most seriously weaken the comparison among treatments, based on Figure 2 and the stated procedure?
choices: It would make the measured oxygen volume independent of the solution concentration.
It would introduce a light exposure difference that could mimic an effect of concentration.
It would cause the initial masses in Table 1 to become unequal.
It would convert the 0 mg/L treatment into a nonexperimental group.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how copper sulfate concentration affects photosynthesis and growth in Elodea sprigs. Three replicate flasks were prepared for each concentration, and the researchers kept the solution volume, initial plant mass, water temperature, lamp distance, and exposure time constant. The 0 mg/L treatment served as the control group. Table 1 gives mean initial and final plant masses, Figure 1 shows oxygen volume collected during the trial, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used for all treatments.
items.explanation: Figure 2 shows that the lamp supplies the light, and the procedure states that lamp distance was held constant. Moving one flask would make light exposure a second changing factor, so its lower oxygen production could not be attributed only to copper sulfate.

per_choice.correct: Figure 2 shows that the lamp supplies the light, and the procedure states that lamp distance was held constant. Moving one flask would make light exposure a second changing factor, so its lower oxygen production could not be attributed only to copper sulfate.
per_choice.trap: The initial masses and control classification do not automatically change when a flask is moved; the problem is the newly unequal light exposure.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Which comparison uses the control group most effectively to support the claim that the 4 mg/L treatment reduced both photosynthetic activity and growth relative to untreated plants?
choices: At 30 minutes, the 4 mg/L group had 3 mL oxygen instead of 18 mL, and its mass change was −0.2 g instead of 1.2 g.
At 30 minutes, the 2 mg/L group had 8 mL oxygen instead of 3 mL, and its final mass was 2.4 g instead of 1.8 g.
The 4 mg/L group began at 2.0 g, and the 0 mg/L group began at 2.0 g.
The 0 mg/L group produced 6 mL oxygen at 10 minutes, and the 1 mg/L group produced 13 mL at 30 minutes.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how copper sulfate concentration affects photosynthesis and growth in Elodea sprigs. Three replicate flasks were prepared for each concentration, and the researchers kept the solution volume, initial plant mass, water temperature, lamp distance, and exposure time constant. The 0 mg/L treatment served as the control group. Table 1 gives mean initial and final plant masses, Figure 1 shows oxygen volume collected during the trial, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used for all treatments.
items.explanation: The control is the 0 mg/L group. Figure 1 provides the 30-minute oxygen values of 3 and 18 mL, while Table 1 provides mass changes of −0.2 and 1.2 g, so this comparison addresses both processes.

per_choice.correct: The control is the 0 mg/L group. Figure 1 provides the 30-minute oxygen values of 3 and 18 mL, while Table 1 provides mass changes of −0.2 and 1.2 g, so this comparison addresses both processes.
per_choice.trap: Choice C shows a constant, not an outcome; choice D compares two treatments at different times and does not establish the control comparison.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Which observation would be most important for deciding whether differences in final mass could be attributed to copper sulfate rather than to unequal starting material?
choices: Every treatment began with an initial mass of 2.0 g, while final masses varied across the concentrations.
The gas tube was attached to the flask before oxygen was collected.
The 0 mg/L treatment produced more oxygen at 30 minutes than the 4 mg/L treatment.
The water bath was drawn between the flask and the lamp in Figure 2.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how copper sulfate concentration affects photosynthesis and growth in Elodea sprigs. Three replicate flasks were prepared for each concentration, and the researchers kept the solution volume, initial plant mass, water temperature, lamp distance, and exposure time constant. The 0 mg/L treatment served as the control group. Table 1 gives mean initial and final plant masses, Figure 1 shows oxygen volume collected during the trial, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used for all treatments.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows that initial mass was 2.0 g for every concentration, so unequal starting plant mass cannot explain the different final masses. The variation occurs after treatment exposure.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: An unknown flask was prepared with the same starting mass and conditions as the others. Its final mass was 2.4 g, and it contained 8 mL of oxygen after 30 minutes. Which copper sulfate concentration was most consistent with both displays?
choices: 0 mg/L
1 mg/L
2 mg/L
4 mg/L
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how copper sulfate concentration affects photosynthesis and growth in Elodea sprigs. Three replicate flasks were prepared for each concentration, and the researchers kept the solution volume, initial plant mass, water temperature, lamp distance, and exposure time constant. The 0 mg/L treatment served as the control group. Table 1 gives mean initial and final plant masses, Figure 1 shows oxygen volume collected during the trial, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used for all treatments.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows a final mass of 2.4 g for 2 mg/L, and Figure 1 shows 8 mL of oxygen at 30 minutes for the same concentration.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 shows a final mass of 2.4 g for 2 mg/L, and Figure 1 shows 8 mL of oxygen at 30 minutes for the same concentration.
per_choice.trap: The final mass alone could invite a comparison with a nearby treatment, but the oxygen value identifies the same 2 mg/L series.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: The researchers want to test whether the copper ion, rather than the sulfate ion, caused the reduction shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. Which additional group would provide the most appropriate comparison?
choices: A group receiving 4 mg/L copper sulfate but with twice the lamp distance
A group receiving no solute but with twice the initial Elodea mass
A group receiving a sulfate compound without copper, with the sulfate amount matched to that in the 4 mg/L treatment
A group receiving 1 mg/L copper sulfate while the water bath is removed
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how copper sulfate concentration affects photosynthesis and growth in Elodea sprigs. Three replicate flasks were prepared for each concentration, and the researchers kept the solution volume, initial plant mass, water temperature, lamp distance, and exposure time constant. The 0 mg/L treatment served as the control group. Table 1 gives mean initial and final plant masses, Figure 1 shows oxygen volume collected during the trial, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used for all treatments.
items.explanation: A sulfate-only group with the same sulfate amount would keep the sulfate component present while removing copper. Comparing it with 4 mg/L copper sulfate could isolate which ion is responsible.

per_choice.correct: A sulfate-only group with the same sulfate amount would keep the sulfate component present while removing copper. Comparing it with 4 mg/L copper sulfate could isolate which ion is responsible.
per_choice.trap: The other choices introduce a new light, starting-mass, or temperature difference, so they would add confounding factors instead of isolating the ion.

items.stem: Which conclusion is best supported when the concentration pattern in Table 1 is considered together with the oxygen pattern in Figure 1, while remembering the constants described in the passage?
choices: Increasing copper sulfate concentration was associated with lower oxygen production and lower mass gain under these conditions.
Copper sulfate prevented all photosynthesis whenever the solution contained at least 1 mg/L.
The decrease in final mass must have been caused by unequal initial plant masses.
Copper sulfate changed plant mass but had no relationship to photosynthetic activity.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how copper sulfate concentration affects photosynthesis and growth in Elodea sprigs. Three replicate flasks were prepared for each concentration, and the researchers kept the solution volume, initial plant mass, water temperature, lamp distance, and exposure time constant. The 0 mg/L treatment served as the control group. Table 1 gives mean initial and final plant masses, Figure 1 shows oxygen volume collected during the trial, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used for all treatments.
items.explanation: Across both displays, increasing concentration corresponds to less oxygen production and progressively smaller mass change, including mass loss at 4 mg/L. The stated constants make the concentration comparison meaningful, but the data do not show that photosynthesis stopped completely at 1 mg/L.

per_choice.trap: The extreme claims confuse reduced activity with no activity, or ignore the equal initial masses and the oxygen trend.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: The reaction time was fixed at 6 min in Table 1. Why was this constant especially necessary for interpreting the foam heights in Figure 1?
choices: It ensured that every mixture had the same pH after the reaction ended.
It prevented the control mixture from being compared with the other mixtures.
It made the buffer volume equal to the yeast volume in every trial.
It ensured that a taller foam column could not simply reflect a longer reaction period.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how pH affects the activity of catalase in yeast. Equal amounts of yeast suspension and hydrogen peroxide were mixed with buffer solutions of different pH values, and foam height was measured after a fixed reaction time. The pH 7 mixture was designated the control, while temperature, reagent volumes, and reaction time were kept constant. Table 1 lists the conditions, Figure 1 shows foam height, and Figure 2 places the tested pH values on the acidic-to-basic scale.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows the same 6-min duration for every trial, so Figure 1 compares foam produced over equal time intervals rather than unequal reaction periods.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 shows the same 6-min duration for every trial, so Figure 1 compares foam produced over equal time intervals rather than unequal reaction periods.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: According to Figures 1 and 2, how much greater was the foam height at the basic pH 9 condition than at the basic pH 11 condition?
choices: 5 mm
8 mm
13 mm
23 mm
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how pH affects the activity of catalase in yeast. Equal amounts of yeast suspension and hydrogen peroxide were mixed with buffer solutions of different pH values, and foam height was measured after a fixed reaction time. The pH 7 mixture was designated the control, while temperature, reagent volumes, and reaction time were kept constant. Table 1 lists the conditions, Figure 1 shows foam height, and Figure 2 places the tested pH values on the acidic-to-basic scale.
items.explanation: Figure 2 identifies both pH 9 and pH 11 as basic. Figure 1 gives heights of 18 mm and 5 mm, respectively; 18 - 5 = 13 mm.

per_choice.correct: Figure 2 identifies both pH 9 and pH 11 as basic. Figure 1 gives heights of 18 mm and 5 mm, respectively; 18 - 5 = 13 mm.
per_choice.trap: Five millimeters is the pH 11 height, 8 mm is the pH 3 height, and 23 mm results from adding the two foam heights.

items.tests: Which factor was held constant, and why a control group exists.

items.stem: Using Table 1 and Figure 1, how much greater was the foam-production rate at pH 5 than at pH 9?
choices: 0.5 mm/min
1.0 mm/min
6.0 mm/min
7.0 mm/min
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how pH affects the activity of catalase in yeast. Equal amounts of yeast suspension and hydrogen peroxide were mixed with buffer solutions of different pH values, and foam height was measured after a fixed reaction time. The pH 7 mixture was designated the control, while temperature, reagent volumes, and reaction time were kept constant. Table 1 lists the conditions, Figure 1 shows foam height, and Figure 2 places the tested pH values on the acidic-to-basic scale.
items.explanation: Figure 1 gives 24 mm at pH 5 and 18 mm at pH 9. Table 1 shows that both were measured after 6 min, so the rate difference is (24 - 18) / 6 = 1.0 mm/min.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 gives 24 mm at pH 5 and 18 mm at pH 9. Table 1 shows that both were measured after 6 min, so the rate difference is (24 - 18) / 6 = 1.0 mm/min.
per_choice.trap: Six millimeters is the difference in foam height without dividing by time; 7.0 mm/min comes from adding the heights before division, and 0.5 uses an incorrect time difference.

items.stem: Which hypothesis is most strongly supported by Figures 1 and 2?
choices: Catalase activity is greatest in acidic solutions and is unaffected by basicity.
Catalase activity is greatest near neutral pH and decreases toward both acidic and basic extremes.
Catalase activity increases continuously as solutions become more basic.
Catalase activity depends only on whether the solution is acidic or basic, not on its particular pH.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how pH affects the activity of catalase in yeast. Equal amounts of yeast suspension and hydrogen peroxide were mixed with buffer solutions of different pH values, and foam height was measured after a fixed reaction time. The pH 7 mixture was designated the control, while temperature, reagent volumes, and reaction time were kept constant. Table 1 lists the conditions, Figure 1 shows foam height, and Figure 2 places the tested pH values on the acidic-to-basic scale.
items.explanation: Figure 2 classifies pH 3 and 5 as acidic, pH 7 as neutral, and pH 9 and 11 as basic. Figure 1 shows the maximum foam height at pH 7 and lower values on both sides.

per_choice.correct: Figure 2 classifies pH 3 and 5 as acidic, pH 7 as neutral, and pH 9 and 11 as basic. Figure 1 shows the maximum foam height at pH 7 and lower values on both sides.

items.stem: Researchers repeat the experiment at 35 C for one additional pH. Which comparison would most directly test whether temperature changes the foam height at pH 9?
choices: Compare pH 11 at 35 C with pH 11 at 25 C, while doubling the reaction time at 35 C.
Compare pH 9 at 35 C with pH 9 at 25 C, keeping reagent volumes and reaction time unchanged.
Compare pH 5 at 35 C with pH 9 at 25 C, keeping the temperature difference as the only change.
Compare pH 9 at 35 C with pH 7 at 25 C, keeping reagent volumes unchanged.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how pH affects the activity of catalase in yeast. Equal amounts of yeast suspension and hydrogen peroxide were mixed with buffer solutions of different pH values, and foam height was measured after a fixed reaction time. The pH 7 mixture was designated the control, while temperature, reagent volumes, and reaction time were kept constant. Table 1 lists the conditions, Figure 1 shows foam height, and Figure 2 places the tested pH values on the acidic-to-basic scale.
items.explanation: Table 1 establishes pH 9 at 25 C as the proper baseline. Comparing it with pH 9 at 35 C changes temperature while preserving the pH and the other listed conditions.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 establishes pH 9 at 25 C as the proper baseline. Comparing it with pH 9 at 35 C changes temperature while preserving the pH and the other listed conditions.
per_choice.trap: The other comparisons also change pH or reaction time, so any foam difference could not be attributed specifically to temperature at pH 9.
